feature_results.rationale: Claude Code documents a native hooks mechanism spanning the agent's action lifecycle generally (not a single narrow event): hooks fire around tool calls (PreToolUse/PostToolUse) as well as other session events, and are evaluated as an explicit step in the permission pipeline (PreToolUse Hook -> Deny Rules -> Allow Rules -> Ask Rules -> Permission Mode Check -> canUseTool Callback -> PostToolUse Hook). Critically, a PreToolUse hook can return a permission decision of 'deny' that blocks the tool call before it executes, and this block applies even in bypassPermissions mode or with --dangerously-skip-permissions, i.e. the user cannot simply switch autonomy mode to escape it. This is a documented, user-supplied-logic mechanism that can influence/block an agent action around tool calls broadly, matching has_criteria and exceeding the partial_criteria ceiling of a single narrow event type.

evidence.excerpt: PreToolUse hooks fire before any permission-mode check, in every permission mode, including dontAsk.

A hook that returns permissionDecision: "deny" blocks the tool even in bypassPermissions mode or with --dangerously-skip-permissions. This lets you enforce policy that users can't bypass by changing their permission mode.

constraints.description: PostToolUse hooks fire only after a tool has already executed and can observe/react (e.g. run checks, log, or surface a warning) but cannot undo or block the already-completed action; blocking is only available via PreToolUse hooks.

queries: Claude Code hooks documentation PreToolUse PostToolUse block permission decision site:docs.claude.com

feature_results.rationale: Claude Code documents a configurable, non-default network-egress control for its agent execution environment beyond generic process isolation: the sandboxed Bash tool provides filesystem and network isolation and restricts which domains sandboxed processes can reach; the Enterprise network configuration page describes proxy allowlisting and firewall rules for the specific domains Claude Code needs; and the reference devcontainer ships an init-firewall.sh script that blocks all outbound traffic except explicitly allowed domains. Together these describe a configurable allow-list mechanism, not merely a fixed default.

evidence.excerpt: Claude Code includes a sandboxed bash tool with filesystem and network isolation. The sandbox restricts which domains processes can connect to, and by default the built-in proxy does not terminate or inspect TLS on outbound traffic.
Claude Code requires access to the following URLs, which should be allowlisted in your proxy configuration and firewall rules, especially in containerized or restricted network environments.
The reference container includes an init-firewall.sh script that blocks all outbound traffic except the domains Claude Code and development tools need.

constraints.description: Documented allow-list/firewall configuration applies to Claude Code's sandboxed execution modes (sandboxed Bash tool, reference devcontainer) and enterprise-managed network deployments, rather than being a single universal toggle across every run mode.

site:docs.claude.com Claude Code network-config "outbound" domains allowlist firewall

feature_results.rationale: Claude Code documents a session-wide checkpoint/rewind mechanism (the /rewind command, or Esc-Esc) that automatically snapshots code state before every user prompt and lets the user restore code and conversation together back to an earlier point in one operation, not merely a single file or hunk. Checkpoints persist with the conversation across resumed sessions.

evidence.excerpt: Checkpointing automatically captures the state of your code before each user prompt... Run /rewind, or press Esc twice when the prompt input is empty, to open the rewind menu... Restore code and conversation (revert both code and conversation to that point)

feature_results.rationale: Claude Code's official GitHub Actions documentation describes a dedicated GitHub Code Review feature that posts automatic reviews on every PR without requiring a manual trigger, in addition to on-demand review via an @claude mention in a PR or issue comment. This is a dedicated review workflow producing review comments/suggestions on diffs, not merely ad-hoc chat, satisfying has_criteria. A GitLab CI/CD equivalent is separately documented.

feature_results.rationale: Claude Code's official 'How Claude Code works' documentation states that because Claude reads the whole project it can handle complex refactoring tasks, feature tracing, and consistency audits across the entire project structure, not just a single file or symbol. The official agents/subagents documentation further describes an explicit large-scale automated-refactoring pattern driven purely by natural-language instruction: for example, deprecating a function used across dozens of files, where a primary agent locates every call site and dedicated sub-agents perform the same instruction-driven replacement in each file. This is a multi-location, instruction-driven refactor rather than a manual IDE-native refactor command and is not limited to single-symbol renames, satisfying has_criteria and exceeding the partial_criteria ceiling.

evidence.excerpt: it can handle complex refactoring tasks, feature tracing, and consistency audits across your entire project structure

For large-scale automated refactoring, like deprecating a function used in 75 files, have a primary agent grep for all instances, then spin up a dedicated sub-agent for each file to perform the replacement in a small, safe context.

constraints.description: The documented large-scale (many-file) refactoring pattern is presented as a sub-agent orchestration technique the user or a skill sets up, rather than a single one-click 'refactor' command.

feature_results.rationale: No official Anthropic source documents a built-in, meaning-based (embedding/semantic) search across the whole Claude Code codebase; the vendor instead documents a deliberate design choice against maintaining any such index. Anthropic's own blog on large codebases states Claude Code 'navigates a codebase the way a software engineer would: it traverses the file system, reads files, uses grep to find exactly what it needs, and follows references across the codebase,' and explicitly contrasts this with RAG-style approaches: 'RAG-powered AI coding tools work by embedding the entire codebase and retrieving relevant chunks at query time... those systems can fail because embedding pipelines can't keep up with active engineering teams... Instead, agentic search avoids those failure modes. There's no embedding pipeline or centralized index to maintain.' The official MCP integration-catalog documentation lists filesystem, GitHub, Context7, Playwright, and Sequential Thinking as featured example servers, with no first-party meaning-based whole-codebase search server. A targeted re-check of the changelog (github.com/anthropics/claude-code CHANGELOG.md and docs.claude.com release notes) surfaced no entry adding semantic/embedding-based codebase search; the only embedding-related hits were unrelated Anthropic cookbook material (VoyageAI embeddings guide, tool-search-with-embeddings notebook, both about a different feature) and open community GitHub feature requests (e.g. issues #28196 and #20836) explicitly asking Anthropic to add local embedding-based semantic search because Claude Code 'currently relies on basic tools like grep and glob' -- itself evidence the capability is not yet shipped. A targeted re-check of the pricing/cost pages (claude.com/pricing, code.claude.com/docs/en/costs) found only usage-cost figures (e.g. per-developer-per-day API spend) and no mention of a semantic-search feature or indexing tier. Third-party MCP servers (e.g. zilliztech/claude-context, community codebase-indexer projects) can bolt on vector-based code search, but per the official-sources-only rule a community integration cannot justify a has/partial status for the vendor's own product. All relevant source classes (documentation, product_page, changelog, pricing, integration_catalog, other) were checked via multiple independent queries with consistent, mutually corroborating results and no conflicting official evidence, so the negative-result protocol is satisfied without any unresolved access gap.

feature_results.rationale: Claude Code documents a file-based, user-authorable custom subagent mechanism: Markdown files with YAML frontmatter stored at the user level (~/.claude/agents/) or project level (.claude/agents/), auto-detected on disk without a restart. Frontmatter fields explicitly include tool-access scoping (tools, disallowedTools), a permission mode, and optional attached MCP servers (mcpServers), alongside the subagent's own prompt/description. This is a documented, supported extension mechanism (not undocumented/experimental) letting the user register a new sub-agent/persona with its own prompt, independent tool scope, and optional MCP attachments, directly matching has_criteria.

evidence.excerpt: Subagents are stored as Markdown files with YAML frontmatter in two locations: User subagents in ~/.claude/agents/ (available across all projects) and project subagents in .claude/agents/ (specific to your project and shareable with your team).

The frontmatter fields available include: description, prompt, tools, disallowedTools, model, permissionMode, mcpServers, hooks, maxTurns, skills, initialPrompt, memory, effort, background, isolation, and color.

feature_results.rationale: The Claude Agent SDK (which underlies Claude Code) documents a dedicated 'custom tools' authoring surface, separate from its MCP-server-connection page: a developer defines a tool's name, handler, input schema, and description via the tool() helper (TypeScript) or @tool decorator (Python). This does not require configuring or running a separate/external MCP server process; the resulting tool is wrapped with createSdkMcpServer/create_sdk_mcp_server and runs in-process inside the calling application. Because the documentation presents this as a distinct, native registration surface (a function/handler definition, not an external server integration) and Claude calls the registered function directly, it matches has_criteria for a mechanism independent of connecting an external MCP server, even though it is implemented under the hood using the MCP protocol in-process.

evidence.excerpt: A tool is defined by four parts, passed as arguments to the tool() helper in TypeScript or the @tool decorator in Python
After defining a tool, wrap it in a server with createSdkMcpServer (TypeScript) or create_sdk_mcp_server (Python). The server runs in-process inside your application, not as a separate process.

constraints.description: Implemented as an in-process MCP server wrapper (createSdkMcpServer / create_sdk_mcp_server) rather than a mechanism wholly unrelated to the MCP protocol; it does not require configuring or running an external MCP server process, unlike ordinary MCP server integrations, but the underlying transport still reuses MCP's tool-call format.
Documented as an Agent SDK capability for building Claude-powered applications programmatically, rather than a setting exposed directly inside the interactive Claude Code CLI chat UI.

feature_results.rationale: Claude Code documents Zero Data Retention (ZDR): when enabled, prompts and model responses generated during Claude Code sessions are processed in real time and not stored by Anthropic after the response is returned. However, ZDR is explicitly documented as not included in the standard Claude for Enterprise plan and cannot be enabled from an organization's own admin settings; it is available only to qualified accounts and requires separate enablement by Anthropic per organization. This matches the partial criterion of an opt-out available only on specific enterprise arrangements rather than a generally available, self-service customer-facing control across tiers. Retained (non-ZDR) commercial data is documented as never used for model training without express permission.

evidence.excerpt: Zero Data Retention (ZDR) for Claude Code is available to qualified accounts on Claude for Enterprise... ZDR is not included in the standard Claude for Enterprise plan and cannot be enabled from your admin settings. It is available to qualified accounts and requires separate enablement by Anthropic.

For commercial users (Team, Enterprise, and API): the standard retention period is 30 days, and zero data retention is available with appropriately configured API keys—Claude Code will not retain chat transcripts on servers.

constraints.description: Zero Data Retention requires a qualified Claude for Enterprise account with separate enablement by Anthropic's account team; it is not a standard self-service admin toggle available to all tiers.

feature_results.rationale: Anthropic's official Help Center article and Claude Code documentation for automated security reviews (/security-review, and the Claude Security plugin) list 'dependency vulnerabilities' -- checks for known issues in third-party packages -- as one of several categories of findings an automated security review surfaces, alongside SQL injection, XSS, authentication flaws, and insecure data handling. This documents some dependency-vulnerability surfacing, satisfying part of has_criteria. However, the same official documentation explicitly frames Claude Security's LLM-driven review as complementary to, not a replacement for, dedicated deterministic 'dependency scanning' (SCA) tooling, and no official page documents integration with a named CVE/vulnerability database or states which package ecosystems/managers are covered. This falls short of a documented CVE-database integration with stated ecosystem coverage, so it is recorded as partial rather than has.

evidence.excerpt: these features check for common security issues including SQL injection risks, cross-site scripting (XSS) vulnerabilities, authentication flaws, insecure data handling, and dependency vulnerabilities

Claude Security should be run alongside static analysis, dependency scanning, and code review, as it reasons about your code the way a human security researcher would, which complements the deterministic checks those tools provide.

constraints.description: Dependency-vulnerability findings are one category surfaced by the broader, LLM-driven /security-review or Claude Security scan rather than a dedicated CVE/vulnerability-database-matched SCA integration; Anthropic's own guidance recommends running it alongside separate, dedicated dependency-scanning tools, and no official page names a specific vulnerability database or enumerates covered package ecosystems.

feature_results.rationale: Claude Code's official interactive-mode documentation states that when Claude wants to edit a file it shows a side-by-side comparison of the original and proposed change and asks for permission before the change is written, with the user able to accept, reject, or redirect Claude, and even edit the proposed diff content directly before accepting. The official permission-modes documentation and product page corroborate this with distinct modes governing per-edit review (default), batched editor/git-diff review after the fact (acceptEdits), or a no-edit planning-only mode (plan), plus the product page's own description of 'inline diffs' and 'plan review' as core interaction mechanics. This is a reviewable diff with accept/reject controls prior to changes being written to disk, satisfying has_criteria at finer than whole-file granularity (per proposed edit, individually editable), so it exceeds the partial_criteria ceiling.

evidence.excerpt: When Claude wants to edit a file, it shows a side-by-side comparison of the original and proposed changes, then asks for permission. You can accept, reject, or tell Claude what to do instead.
Use acceptEdits when you want to review changes in your editor or via git diff after the fact rather than approving each edit inline.
Claude Code provides AI coding assistance with inline diffs, @-mentions, plan review, and keyboard shortcuts.

constraints.description: The bypassPermissions mode approves all edits (and is inherited by all subagents) with no per-edit or batched diff review step, so the reviewable-diff workflow can be deliberately disabled by configuration.

feature_results.rationale: No official Anthropic source documents Claude Code operating with zero network connectivity for its core functionality. The official enterprise network-configuration documentation states the product must reach api.anthropic.com (or an equivalent Bedrock/Vertex/Azure endpoint) for model inference, MCP servers for tool calls, and target hosts for WebFetch, and describes only proxying/allow-listing that traffic rather than eliminating it; no documentation, product, changelog, or pricing page describes a fully offline or air-gapped operating mode. The official CHANGELOG.md and release notes contain no entry introducing offline/air-gapped support (the only offline-adjacent changelog item concerns a plugin marketplace cache fallback, unrelated to core model connectivity). The pricing/enterprise pages describe deployment through a customer's own Bedrock/Vertex/Azure account, which still requires reaching a model-serving endpoint over the network, not zero-network operation. Two open GitHub feature requests in the product's own repository (asking for 'Complete Offline Installation' and for air-gapped-friendly distribution URLs) further indicate this is a requested-but-unimplemented capability rather than a documented feature. A third-party community project claiming fully offline operation via a locally hosted model is unofficial and, even if taken at face value, would fall under the taxonomy's explicit exclusion for a swappable local model (local_offline_model_support) rather than this feature. All relevant source classes were checked and none surfaced supporting evidence.

additional_facts.description: Claude Code does not ship a bundled code formatter or linter by default. Static-analysis/lint feedback is delivered through the general-purpose Hooks mechanism instead: a documented example wires a PostToolUse hook to run eslint against newly edited TypeScript/JavaScript files and feed failures back to Claude, but the user must configure both the hook and the underlying linter/formatter themselves.

evidence.excerpt: A PostToolUse hook can lint new TypeScript/JavaScript files by checking the file extension and running eslint with max-warnings set to 0.

additional_facts.description: Commercial (Team, Enterprise, API) Claude Code usage carries a documented standard 30-day data retention period, with zero data retention available given appropriately configured API keys. Organizations separately get a Compliance API activity feed giving audit-level visibility into SSO sign-ins, API-key lifecycle, and console activity, and Anthropic's Data Processing Addendum grants customers a general, advance-notice-backed authorization to engage the sub-processors it itemizes in a dedicated schedule.

evidence.excerpt: For commercial users (Team, Enterprise, and API): the standard retention period is 30 days, and zero data retention is available with appropriately configured API keys—Claude Code will not retain chat transcripts on servers.

The Compliance API gives Claude Enterprise customers programmatic access to their organization's Activity Feed... security and compliance teams can monitor SSO sign-ins and authentication events, track API key lifecycle, audit console activity including member invites and role changes, and investigate Claude usage at the audit level.

additional_facts.description: Some governance-oriented capabilities are restricted specifically to Claude for Enterprise rather than being available across all paid tiers: SSO/domain capture, role-based permissions, and managed policy settings for organization-wide configuration are documented under Claude for Enterprise, and Zero Data Retention is explicitly excluded from the standard Enterprise plan - it requires separate, per-organization enablement by Anthropic rather than a self-service admin setting.

evidence.excerpt: Claude for Enterprise adds SSO and domain capture, role-based permissions, compliance API access, and managed policy settings for deploying organization-wide Claude Code configurations.

Zero Data Retention (ZDR) for Claude Code is available to qualified accounts on Claude for Enterprise... additional_facts.description: Beyond connecting to hundreds of external tools and data sources via the Model Context Protocol, with pre-built servers available for systems such as Google Drive, Slack, GitHub, Git, Postgres, and Puppeteer, the Claude Agent SDK documents a distinct in-process custom-tool-authoring surface - the tool() helper in TypeScript or the @tool decorator in Python - that registers a function-based tool without configuring or running a separate MCP server process, wrapped under the hood via createSdkMcpServer/create_sdk_mcp_server.

evidence.excerpt: Claude Code can connect to hundreds of external tools and data sources through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open source standard for AI-tool integrations.
Pre-built MCP servers are available for popular enterprise systems like Google Drive, Slack, GitHub, Git, Postgres, and Puppeteer.
After defining a tool, wrap it in a server with createSdkMcpServer (TypeScript) or create_sdk_mcp_server (Python). The server runs in-process inside your application, not as a separate process.

additional_facts.description: Claude Code documents more than one concurrency pattern beyond single-subagent delegation: a lead agent can spawn multiple subagents to work on different parts of a task simultaneously, assigning subtasks and merging their results, while separately a user can run fully independent parallel sessions - via git worktrees so concurrent edits don't collide, separate tabs/windows, or multiple simultaneous `--cloud` invocations, each running as its own independent cloud session.

evidence.excerpt: You can spawn multiple Claude Code agents that work on different parts of a task simultaneously, with a lead agent coordinating the work, assigning subtasks, and merging results.
Each `--cloud` command creates its own cloud session that runs independently, and you can start multiple tasks that will all run simultaneously in separate sessions.

additional_facts.description: Custom subagents are defined as Markdown files with YAML frontmatter, stored at the user level (~/.claude/agents/, available across all projects) or the project level (.claude/agents/, shareable with a team), and are auto-detected on disk without a restart. Frontmatter fields scope each subagent independently, including its own tool access (tools, disallowedTools), permission mode, and optionally attached MCP servers.

evidence.excerpt: Subagents are stored as Markdown files with YAML frontmatter in two locations: User subagents in ~/.claude/agents/ (available across all projects) and project subagents in .claude/agents/ (specific to your project and shareable with your team).

The frontmatter fields available include: description, prompt, tools, disallowedTools, model, permissionMode, mcpServers, hooks, maxTurns, skills, initialPrompt, memory, effort, background, isolation, and color.

use_cases.title: Automate recurring maintenance work on a schedule
use_cases.description: An organization configures a recurring cloud Routine (or a Desktop scheduled task) that runs a saved Claude Code prompt against a repository on a schedule, e.g. nightly, with long-running steps able to run in the background so they don't block the session - useful for tasks like dependency updates or periodic security-review sweeps.
use_cases.rationale: Scheduled recurring task execution and background long-running task handling are each documented individually as first-party mechanisms designed to compose into unattended, recurring maintenance automation, even though no single official page walks through this exact combined workflow.

use_cases.title: Automated GitHub PR review and PR creation
use_cases.description: Claude Code's GitHub Actions integration posts automatic code reviews on every pull request without a manual trigger (or on demand via an @claude mention), and separately can create pull requests directly, with read & write permissions specifically to open PRs and push changes rather than requiring a manual follow-up step by the developer.

evidence.excerpt: For automatic reviews posted on every PR without a trigger, there is a GitHub Code Review feature.
Pull requests have read & write permissions to create PRs and push changes.

use_cases.title: Generate unit tests across a codebase
use_cases.description: A developer asks Claude Code to write unit tests; Anthropic's own explainer describes it generating, refining, and managing high-quality unit tests across both frontend and backend codebases, targeting the developer's existing stack rather than a fixed test format.

evidence.excerpt: Claude Code is an agentic coding tool that integrates with your development environment and generates, refines, and manages high-quality unit tests across frontend and backend codebases.

use_cases.title: Governed enterprise rollout with sandboxing, private deployment, and audit oversight
use_cases.description: A platform team rolls out Claude Code organization-wide with SSO and managed policy settings, runs agent commands inside OS-level sandboxes with a restricted network egress allow-list, keeps model traffic inside its own Amazon Bedrock, Vertex AI, or Microsoft Foundry account, and relies on documented data-retention controls together with Compliance API audit trails for oversight.
use_cases.rationale: Enterprise SSO/RBAC, sandboxed and network-restricted execution, customer-cloud private deployment, documented retention controls, and organization audit logging are each individually documented features that combine naturally into a single governed enterprise deployment pattern, even though no one official page frames this exact combined scenario.

use_cases.title: Large-scale, instruction-driven refactor across many files
use_cases.description: A developer describes a refactor in plain language, such as deprecating a function used across dozens of files; the documented pattern has a primary agent grep for every call site and then spin up a dedicated sub-agent per file to perform the same replacement in a small, safe context, rather than a manual per-file IDE refactor.

evidence.excerpt: For large-scale automated refactoring, like deprecating a function used in 75 files, have a primary agent grep for all instances, then spin up a dedicated sub-agent for each file to perform the replacement in a small, safe context.

use_cases.title: Onboard onto and navigate a large, unfamiliar codebase
use_cases.description: An engineer joining a large monorepo relies on Claude Code's automatic conversation-compaction, vendor guidance for large codebases (running an LSP server for symbol-based search, maintaining a lightweight codebase map, scoping work to subdirectories), and layered CLAUDE.md instruction files to explore the codebase and retain project conventions across sessions; because no built-in embedding-based semantic search is documented, this relies on native grep/glob-based agentic search rather than a whole-repo meaning-based index.
use_cases.rationale: Long-context/large-repo handling and layered, automatically-applied instruction precedence are each documented individually and combine to support exploratory onboarding, even though no single official page frames this exact end-to-end scenario; the absence of built-in semantic search is noted because it is directly relevant to how this use case is actually carried out.

use_cases.title: Run highly autonomous coding sessions under enforced guardrails
use_cases.description: A team runs Claude Code in a highly autonomous permission mode for speed, while relying on PreToolUse hooks to enforce policy the user cannot bypass by switching modes, upfront plan-mode review requiring explicit approval before execution begins, and granular per-tool/per-pattern permission rules in settings.json to keep the agent's autonomy scoped.
use_cases.rationale: Hooks that can deny a tool call even in bypassPermissions mode, upfront plan-mode review via ExitPlanMode, and fine-grained per-tool permission rules are each documented individually and are designed to compose into exactly this kind of guardrailed-autonomy workflow, though no single official page walks through the combined scenario end-to-end.
